default 100,000,000 tuples (caps the threshold for very large tables)
default typically 16 slots (might be less if kernel settings do not support it, as determined during initdb); autovacuum_max_workers can be changed up to this without restart
200 million transactions (multixact: 400 million)
1.6 billion transactions; settable 0 to 2.1 billion, silently raised to at least 105% of autovacuum_freeze_max_age

vacuum every table at least once every two billion transactions; WARNING when oldest XIDs reach forty million transactions from the wraparound point; system refuses to assign new XIDs once fewer than three million transactions left ('database is not accepting commands that assign new transaction IDs to avoid wraparound data loss'); read-only transactions can still start and VACUUM runs normally
note: Note: 'In earlier versions, it was sometimes necessary to stop the postmaster and VACUUM the database in a single-user mode. In typical scenarios, this is no longer necessary, and should be avoided whenever possible'; only reason is to TRUNCATE or DROP unneeded tables. XIDs are 32 bits, compared modulo 2^32.

value: default -1: replication slots may retain an unlimited amount of WAL; otherwise a slot whose restart_lsn falls behind by more than the size may lose required WAL
note: Added in PG13; WAL availability visible in pg_replication_slots

value: invalidates slots inactive longer than this; default 0 disables; invalidation happens at checkpoint; uses pg_replication_slots.inactive_since
typically 100 connections (might be less if kernel settings do not support it); server start only
default typically 128 megabytes (128MB); dedicated server with 1GB+ RAM: reasonable start is 25% of memory; more than 40% of RAM unlikely to work better
four megabytes (4MB) per sort/hash operation; total can be many times work_mem; hash_mem_multiplier default 2.0

statement_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, transaction_timeout all default 0 (disabled), unit milliseconds; idle in transaction prevents vacuuming recently-dead tuples (bloat); setting statement_timeout or transaction_timeout in postgresql.conf is not recommended because it affects all sessions
note: transaction_timeout added in PG17; prepared transactions are not subject to it

value: replica (minimal, replica, logical); logical needed for logical decoding

archive_command: shell command with %p (path) and %f (file name), must return zero only on success; archive_library: shared library alternative, empty default means archive_command is used; setting both raises an error
recovery_target_time: timestamp up to which recovery proceeds (stopping point also set by recovery_target_inclusive); recovery_target_action default pause, alternatives promote and shutdown

remote_apply, on (the default), remote_write, local, off; with empty synchronous_standby_names only on and off are meaningful; off can lose recent commits (max delay three times wal_writer_delay) but no inconsistency
[FIRST] num_sync ( standby_name [, ...] ) priority-based; ANY num_sync ( standby_name [, ...] ) quorum-based; or plain standby_name list
note: Example in docs: FIRST 3 (s1, s2, s3, s4)

value: Incremental backups can be created using pg_basebackup's new --incremental option; new application pg_combinebackup allows manipulation of base and incremental file system backups; relies on WAL summarization files (summarize_wal)
note: PG18 adds pg_combinebackup -k/--link for hard linking

value: new application to create a logical replica from a physical standby server
pg_upgrade now preserves logical replication slots on publishers and full subscription state on subscribers; only works for old clusters that are version 17 or later
note: So it helps for upgrades from 17 onward, not from 16 to 17

value: --swap moves data directories from old to new cluster then replaces catalog files; can outperform --link, --clone, --copy and --copy-file-range, especially with many relations; recommend --sync-method=fsync with --swap. PG18 release: 'pg_upgrade now retains optimizer statistics' (opt out with --no-statistics)
note: Release notes: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/release-18.html . Retained stats are planner stats; cumulative pg_stat_* counters are not mentioned. vacuumdb --missing-stats-only added to fill gaps.

value: Database schema and DDL commands are not replicated; sequence data is not replicated; large objects are not replicated; only tables (including partitioned) can be replicated, not views, materialized views or foreign tables; TRUNCATE across FK-linked tables outside the subscription fails
note: For failover to a subscriber, sequences must be updated to latest values

value: initdb now enables data checksums by default; disable with --no-data-checksums; pg_upgrade requires matching checksum settings
Support for MD5 passwords will be removed in a future major version; CREATE ROLE and ALTER ROLE emit deprecation warnings (disable via md5_password_warnings = off)
PG14 changed default of password_encryption to scram-sha-256 (previously md5); PG18 docs: 'The default is scram-sha-256'
note: Current docs: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/runtime-config-connection.html

claim: Features that break in transaction mode

value: PostgreSQL implements a 'process per user' client/server model: every client process connects to exactly one backend process; the postmaster spawns a new backend for each connection

Microsoft blog, published Oct 8, 2020: with huge_pages, memory overhead of each connection is below 2 MiB ('connection memory overhead is acceptable'); main bottleneck is snapshot scalability in GetSnapshotData() (one active connection with 5000 idle connections slowed by more than 2x); addressed in Postgres 14
note: Corrects the common belief that per-backend memory is the main cost

value: GitLab docs configure PgBouncer in front of PostgreSQL (pool_mode 'transaction' example per database); Heroku: 'Transaction Pooling Mode (Recommended)', pooler assigns a server connection when a transaction begins and releases it when it ends

value: Evan Klitzke, July 26, 2016: write amplification (all indexes updated on row update), verbose physical replication across data centers, a replica bug that misapplied WAL records (data corruption), replica MVCC issues killing long transactions, and upgrades between major versions needing many hours of downtime (stuck on 9.2)
note: Read via WebFetch summary (curl got 406); wording paraphrased, check before quoting

value: 'Sharding Postgres at Notion', 2021-10-06: 480 logical shards (Postgres schemas, 15 per database) evenly distributed across 32 physical databases; TXID wraparound was described as 'an existential threat to the product' and a driver for sharding

'How Figma's databases team lived to tell the scale', 2024-03-14: in 2020 a single Postgres database on AWS's largest physical instance; by end of 2022 a dozen vertically partitioned databases plus caching and read replicas; database stack grew almost 100x since 2020; then horizontal sharding behind PgBouncer and a query engine

'Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY does not scale', published 2025-07-01: a NOTIFY in a transaction acquires a global lock on the entire database during commit, serializing all commits; under many concurrent writers this caused major downtime (logs from 2025-03-22 show AccessExclusiveLock on object 0 of class 1262 waits around 1 s)
note: Post now carries an update saying a Postgres core commit eliminated the bottleneck; which release ships it (likely 19) was not checked
